title: Quarks: Is That All There Is?
lead: Quarks are the fundamental particles that hadrons are made of. This section names the six quark flavors and their fractional charges, shows how baryons and mesons are built from quarks and how their quantum numbers add, and sets out the evidence for quarks, the quantum number called color, and the three families of fundamental particles.
objectives: Outline the quark composition of hadrons.
Determine quantum numbers from quark composition.
summary_html:
• Hadrons are thought to be composed of quarks, with baryons having three quarks and mesons having a quark and an antiquark.
  • The characteristics of the six quarks and their antiquark counterparts are given in Table 33.3, and the quark compositions of certain hadrons are given in Table 33.4.
  • Indirect evidence for quarks is very strong, explaining all known hadrons and their quantum numbers, such as strangeness, charm, topness, and bottomness.
  • Quarks come in six flavors and three colors and occur only in combinations that produce white.
  • Fundamental particles have no further substructure, not even a size beyond their de Broglie wavelength.
  • There are three types of fundamental particles—leptons, quarks, and carrier particles. Each type is divided into three analogous families as indicated in Figure 33.20.
notes: The graph of the Δ⁺⁺ resonance is left out with the unkeyed problem it serves, and the book’s slips are carried as printed: the glossary defines color as “a quark flavor”, a conceptual question asks about mesons of composition “W⁻ or tt̄”, one key writes “Z==0+(−1)”, and the text reads “as seen in Table 33.2).” and “Unification of Forces..”.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s own key. Eleven unkeyed problems are left out: the lifetime of the Δ⁺⁺ from its resonance graph, the decay Ω⁻ → Ξ⁰ + π⁻, the decay η⁰ → γ + γ, whether n → e⁺ + e⁻ is possible, the decay Λ⁰ → n + π⁰, the color combinations of a white meson, the conjectured decay of the proton and of the antiproton, the quantum numbers of the proton and neutron, those of the J/ψ and ϒ, the quarks of the B⁻ meson, and the integral charges of all baryons and mesons. Two keyed problems lean on a left-out one, so each prompt also gives what the left-out problem says. The conceptual questions on the evidence for electroweak unification and on whether gluons are confined are set in 33.6, which introduces those ideas. The fourteen conceptual questions and the unkeyed AP item on the Ω⁻ trace carry AI-marked suggested approaches. The module prints no Check Your Understanding box, so nothing is set inline.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 33.15) All baryons, such as the proton and neutron shown here, are composed of three quarks. All mesons, such as the pions shown here, are composed of a quark-antiquark pair. Arrows represent the spins of the quarks, which, as we shall see, are also colored. The colors are such that they need to add to white for any possible combination of quarks. (Figure 33.19) The three quarks composing a baryon must be RGB, which add to white. The quark and antiquark composing a meson must be a color and anticolor, here RR̄ also adding to white. The force between systems that have color is so great that they can neither be separated nor exist as colored.

Scattering of high-energy electrons from protons at facilities like SLAC produces evidence of three point-like charges consistent with proposed quark properties. This experiment is analogous to Rutherford’s discovery of the small size of the nucleus by scattering α particles. High-energy electrons are used so that the probe wavelength is small enough to see details smaller than the proton.
The three types of particles are leptons, quarks, and carrier particles. Each of those types is divided into three analogous families, with the graviton left out.

exercises.prompt: How many pointlike particles would an experiment scattering high energy electrons from any meson discover within the meson?

answer.hint: Electrons scattered from a proton find its three quarks. What is a meson made of?

exercises.prompt: In this figure, a $K^{-}$ initially hits a proton, and creates three new particles. Identify them, and explain how quark flavors are conserved.

answer.solution: The labels on the trace show the $K^{-}$ striking a proton at rest and leaving three new tracks, the $\Omega^{-}$, a $K^{+}$ and a neutral $K^{0}$: $K^{-}+p\to\Omega^{-}+K^{+}+K^{0}$. Write each in quarks from Table 33.4: $(\bar{u}s)+(uud)\to(sss)+(u\bar{s})+(d\bar{s})$. Before the collision the $\bar{u}$ cancels one $u$, leaving a net one up, one down and one strange quark. After it, the three $s$ of the $\Omega^{-}$ and the two $\bar{s}$ of the kaons leave a net one strange quark, with one up and one down. The collision proceeds by the strong force, which cannot change a quark’s flavor; it only creates quark–antiquark pairs, here two $s\bar{s}$ pairs, so the net number of each flavor is unchanged, and strangeness, $-1$ before and $-3+1+1=-1$ after, is conserved with it.

figure.alt: Particle interaction diagram showing K-, K0, K+, Omega-, Xi0, Lambda0, pi-, p, and gamma particles, with decay paths indicated by dashed lines and a 10 cm scale.

exercises.prompt: The quark flavor change $d\to u$ takes place in $\beta^{-}$ decay. Does this mean that the reverse quark flavor change $u\to d$ takes place in $\beta^{+}$ decay? Justify your response by writing the decay in terms of the quark constituents, noting that it looks as if a proton is converted into a neutron in $\beta^{+}$ decay.

answer.solution:
Yes. In $ eta^{+}$ decay a proton in the nucleus becomes a neutron, $p	o n+ eta^{+}+
u_{e}$. In quarks this is $uud	o udd+ eta^{+}+
u_{e}$: two of the quarks are untouched, and one up quark has become a down quark, $u	o d+ eta^{+}+
u_{e}$. Check it: the charge goes from $+ rac{2}{3}q_{e}$ to $- rac{1}{3}q_{e}+q_{e}=+ rac{2}{3}q_{e}$, and the electron family number is $0=-1+1$. The weak force, which can change any flavor, does it.

exercises.prompt: Explain how the weak force can change strangeness by changing quark flavor.

answer.solution: Strangeness is carried only by strange quarks, $S=-1$ for each $s$ and $+1$ for each $\bar{s}$. The weak force can change a quark’s flavor, so it can turn an $s$ into a $u$ or a $d$, as in $s\to u$ and $s\to d$. Each such change removes a strange quark and so changes the particle’s strangeness by one; the decay $\Lambda^{0}\to p+\pi^{-}$ is an example, $uds\to uud+\bar{u}d$. The strong and electromagnetic forces cannot change flavor, which is why only the weak force violates the conservation of strangeness.

exercises.prompt: Beta decay is caused by the weak force, as are all reactions in which strangeness changes. Does this imply that the weak force can change quark flavor? Explain.

answer.solution: Yes. Write $\beta^{-}$ decay in quarks: $udd\to uud+\beta^{-}+\bar{\nu}_{e}$, which is a down quark becoming an up quark. A change of strangeness likewise means a strange quark has become another flavor, or been made from one. Both are flavor changes, and both are always caused by the weak force, so the weak force must be able to change flavor, while the strong force, which never changes strangeness, cannot.

exercises.prompt: Why is it easier to see the properties of the c, b, and t quarks in mesons having composition $W^{-}$ or $t\bar{t}$ rather than in baryons having a mixture of quarks, such as udb?

answer.solution: Read the question as meaning mesons made of a single flavor, such as $c\bar{c}$ (the $J/\psi$), $b\bar{b}$ (the $\Upsilon$) or $t\bar{t}$. Such a meson is a quark and its own antiquark, so everything measured about it, its mass, its charge, its decays, comes from that one flavor alone; the text calls them bare charm and bare bottom for this reason. In a baryon such as $udb$ the heavy quark’s properties are mixed with those of the up and down quarks and of the forces among all three, so they are harder to pick out.

exercises.prompt: How can quarks, which are fermions, combine to form bosons? Why must an even number combine to form a boson? Give one example by stating the quark substructure of a boson.

answer.solution: Each quark has spin $\frac{1}{2}$, and spins add, so a group of quarks has a total spin made of halves. An even number of halves can add to a whole number, and a particle with integral spin is a boson; an odd number always leaves a half, a fermion. So bosons are made of an even number of quarks, and the mesons are the example: the $\pi^{+}$ is $u\bar{d}$, with the two spins antiparallel, $+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}=0$.

exercises.prompt: What evidence is cited to support the contention that the gluon force between quarks is greater than the strong nuclear force between hadrons? How is this related to color? Is it also related to quark confinement?

answer.solution: The evidence is that no quark has ever been freed: when large energies are put into separating quarks, they are pulled only so far before the energy turns into new particles, which come out in jets, while hadrons can be knocked out of nuclei. The text relates this to color: a white combination exerts only the leftover strong force, like the weak polarization forces of a neutral molecule, but a combination that is not white would exert extremely large forces, larger than the strong force. That is the theory of quark confinement, which explains why quarks exist yet cannot be isolated.

exercises.prompt: Discuss how we know that $\pi \text{-mesons}$ ($\pi^{+},\pi ,\pi^{0}$) are not fundamental particles and are not the basic carriers of the strong force.

answer.solution: A fundamental particle has no substructure, but each pion is made of a quark and an antiquark, the $\pi^{+}$ being $u\bar{d}$ and the $\pi^{-}$ being $\bar{u}d$, as their charges, baryon numbers and spins confirm; scattering experiments find point-like quarks inside hadrons, and the pions decay into other particles. The carrier particles are thought to be fundamental, so a particle with substructure cannot be the basic carrier. Pions are exchanged between nucleons, but the strong force they carry comes from the gluons acting among their quarks.

exercises.prompt: An antibaryon has three antiquarks with colors $\bar{R}\bar{G}\bar{B}$. What is its color?

answer.solution: White. The anticolors antired, antigreen and antiblue are cyan, magenta and yellow, and the three together combine to white, as the three primary colors of a baryon do. An antibaryon must be white for the same reason a baryon must.

exercises.prompt: Suppose leptons are created in a reaction. Does this imply the weak force is acting? (for example, consider $\beta$ decay.)

answer.solution: Not necessarily. In $\beta$ decay an electron and a neutrino are created, and that is the weak force at work, as it is whenever a neutrino appears or a quark changes flavor. But a $\gamma$ ray can create an electron–positron pair by the electromagnetic force alone. Look at what else happens: a lepton created with its own antilepton from a photon needs no weak force, while a lepton created with a neutrino, or with a change of flavor, does.

exercises.prompt: How can the lifetime of a particle indicate that its decay is caused by the strong nuclear force? How can a change in strangeness imply which force is responsible for a reaction? What does a change in quark flavor imply about the force that is responsible?

answer.solution: The stronger the force causing a decay, the faster it acts, so a decay by the strong force gives a very short lifetime, of the order of $10^{-23}\;\text{s}$, while weak decays take $10^{-10}\;\text{s}$ or longer. Strangeness is conserved by the strong and electromagnetic forces, so a reaction that changes it must be caused by the weak force. A change of quark flavor likewise implies the weak force, the only force that can change flavor.

exercises.prompt: (a) Do all particles having strangeness also have at least one strange quark in them? (b) Do all hadrons with a strange quark also have nonzero strangeness?

answer.solution: (a) Strangeness is carried only by strange quarks, so a particle with strangeness must contain at least one strange quark or antiquark; the $K^{+}$, $u\bar{s}$, has $S=+1$ from its antistrange quark. (b) No. Strangeness is the sum over the quarks, so a strange quark and a strange antiquark together, $s\bar{s}$, give $S=-1+1=0$, and a hadron made that way has a strange quark but no strangeness.

exercises.prompt: The sigma-zero particle decays mostly via the reaction $\Sigma^{0}\to \Lambda^{0}+\gamma$. Explain how this decay and the respective quark compositions imply that the $\Sigma^{0}$ is an excited state of the $\Lambda^{0}$.

answer.solution: Table 33.4 gives both particles the same quarks, $uds$. The decay emits only a photon, as an excited atom or nucleus does when it drops to a lower state: no quark changes flavor, and only energy is carried away. The $\Sigma^{0}$’s rest mass, 1192.6 MeV/$c^{2}$, exceeds the $\Lambda^{0}$’s, 1115.7 MeV/$c^{2}$, by the photon’s energy, so the $\Sigma^{0}$ is the same set of quarks in a higher-energy state.

exercises.prompt: What do the quark compositions and other quantum numbers imply about the relationships between the $\Delta^{+}$ and the proton? The $\Delta^{0}$ and the neutron?

answer.solution: The $\Delta^{+}$ and the proton are both $uud$, and the $\Delta^{0}$ and the neutron both $udd$, so each pair has the same charge, baryon number and strangeness. Baryons composed of the same quarks are different states of the same particle: the $\Delta^{+}$ is an excited state of the proton and the $\Delta^{0}$ of the neutron, heavier by the energy of excitation and short-lived, since they decay by the strong force.

exercises.prompt: Discuss the similarities and differences between the photon and the $Z^{0}$ in terms of particle properties, including forces felt.

answer.solution: Both are carrier particles and bosons, both are neutral, and each is its own antiparticle. The photon is massless and carries the electromagnetic force, whose range is infinite; the $Z^{0}$ has a rest mass of $91.19\times 10^{3}\;\text{MeV}/c^{2}$, which limits the weak force it carries to a very short range, and it is unstable, with a lifetime of about $10^{-25}\;\text{s}$. Being neutral, neither feels an electric force; the $Z^{0}$ takes part in the weak interaction, and the photon interacts with charged particles.

exercises.prompt: (a) Verify from its quark composition that the $\Delta^{+}$ particle could be an excited state of the proton. (b) There is a spread of about 100 MeV in the decay energy of the $\Delta^{+}$, interpreted as uncertainty due to its short lifetime. What is its approximate lifetime? (c) Does its decay proceed via the strong or weak force?

answer.hint: Take $\Delta E = 100\;\text{MeV}$ in $\Delta E\,\Delta t\approx h/4\pi$.
answer.solution: (a) The $\text{uud}$ composition is the same as for a proton. (b) $3.3\times 10^{-24}\;\text{s}$ (c) Strong (short lifetime)

exercises.prompt: The preceding problem describes the reaction $\pi^{+}+p\to \Delta^{++}\to \pi^{+}+p$, where the $\Delta^{++}$ is a very short-lived particle. The reaction $\pi^{+}+p\to \Delta^{++}$ (described in the preceding problem) takes place via the strong force. (a) What is the baryon number of the $\Delta^{++}$ particle? (b) Draw a Feynman diagram of the reaction showing the individual quarks involved.

answer.hint: The $\Delta^{++}$ is $uuu$; add the baryon numbers of its quarks.
answer.solution: a) $\Delta^{++}(\text{uuu});\;B=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}=1$ b)

exercises.prompt: Repeat the previous problem for the decay mode $\Omega^{-}\to \Lambda^{0}+K^{-}.$ The previous problem asks: (a) What is the change in strangeness? (b) Verify that baryon number and charge are conserved, while lepton numbers are unaffected. (c) Write the equation in terms of the constituent quarks, indicating that the weak force is responsible.

answer.hint: Read the strangeness of each particle from Table 33.2 and subtract the total before from the total after.
answer.solution: (a) $+1$ (b) $B=1=1+0,Z==0+(-1)$, all lepton numbers are 0 before and after (c) $(\text{sss})\to (\text{uds})+(\bar{u}s)$

exercises.prompt: One decay mode for the eta-zero meson is $\eta^{0}\to \pi^{0}+\pi^{0}$. (a) Write the decay in terms of the quark constituents. (b) How much energy is released? (c) What is the ultimate release of energy, given the decay mode for the pi zero is $\pi^{0}\to \gamma+\gamma$?

answer.solution: (a) $(u\bar{u}+d\bar{d})\to (u\bar{u}+d\bar{d})+(u\bar{u}+d\bar{d})$ (b) 277.9 MeV (c) 547.9 MeV

parts.hint: Subtract the rest energies of the two $\pi^{0}$ from that of the $\eta^{0}$, from Table 33.2.
Once both $\pi^{0}$ have become $\gamma$ rays, all of the $\eta^{0}$’s rest energy has been released.

exercises.prompt: Is the decay $\mu^{-}\to e^{-}+\nu_{e}+\nu_{\mu}$ possible considering the appropriate conservation laws? State why or why not.

answer.solution: No. $\text{Charge}=-1$ is conserved. $L_{e_{\text{i}}}=0\ne L_{e_{\text{f}}}=2$ is not conserved. $L_{\mu}=1$ is conserved.

exercises.prompt: (a) Is the decay $\Sigma^{-}\to n+\pi^{-}$ possible considering the appropriate conservation laws? State why or why not. (b) Write the decay in terms of the quark constituents of the particles.

answer.solution: (a) Yes. $Z=-1=0+(-1)$, $B=1=1+0$, all lepton family numbers are 0 before and after, spontaneous since mass greater before reaction. (b) $\text{dds}\to \text{udd}+\bar{u}d$

exercises.prompt: (a) Three quarks form a baryon. How many combinations of the six known quarks are there if all combinations are possible? (b) This number is less than the number of known baryons. Explain why.

answer.hint: Each of the three quarks may be any of the six flavors.
answer.solution: (a) 216 (b) There are more baryons observed because we have the 6 antiquarks and various mixtures of quarks (as for the $\pi$-meson) as well.

exercises.prompt: Verify the quantum numbers given for the $\Omega^{+}$ in Table 33.2 by adding the quantum numbers for its quark constituents as inferred from Table 33.4.

(a) How much energy would be released if the proton did decay via the conjectured reaction $p\to \pi^{0}+e^{+}$? (b) Given that the $\pi^{0}$ decays to two $\gamma$ s and that the $e^{+}$ will find an electron to annihilate, what total energy is ultimately produced in proton decay? (c) Why is this energy greater than the proton’s total mass (converted to energy)?

answer.solution: (a) 803 MeV (b) 938.8 MeV (c) The annihilation energy of an extra electron is included in the total energy.

parts.hint: Subtract the rest energies of the $\pi^{0}$ and the $e^{+}$ from the proton’s, from Table 33.2.
Add the rest energy of the electron the positron annihilates to the proton’s whole rest energy.

exercises.prompt: There are particles called D-mesons. One of them is the $D^{+}$ meson, which has a single positive charge and a baryon number of zero, also the value of its strangeness, topness, and bottomness. It has a charm of $+1.$ What is its quark configuration?

answer.solution: $c\bar{d}$

exercises.prompt: (a) What particle has the quark composition $\bar{u}\bar{u}\bar{d}$? (b) What should its decay mode be?

answer.solution: a) The antiproton b) $\bar{p}\to \pi^{0}+e^{-}$
